description: How machines talk: packets, addresses, protocols, names, routes, and the physical and wireless links underneath.

concepts.title: Networks
concepts.summary: Machines joined so they can send each other data. The interesting part is not the wires but the agreements: who speaks when, in what format, and what happens when a message gets lost.

concepts.title: Packets
concepts.summary: Data cut into small, labeled pieces that travel separately and are reassembled at the far end. It's why one broken link doesn't break a whole conversation, and why the network can be shared by everyone at once.

concepts.title: Layers
concepts.summary: A way of splitting networking into stacked jobs: wires, addresses, delivery, conversations, applications. Each layer only talks to the one above and below, which is why you can swap Wi-Fi for cable without touching your browser.

concepts.title: Ethernet
concepts.summary: The wired standard that connects most local networks: frames sent over cable between devices addressed by hardware identifiers. Fifty years on, it is still the base most other networks are built on.

concepts.title: Wi-Fi
concepts.summary: Ethernet's wireless cousin, using radio to reach devices in a room or a building. Every device shares the same air, so the standard is largely about taking turns without colliding.

concepts.title: Cellular
concepts.summary: Coverage split into cells, each with its own antenna, so the same radio frequencies can be reused across a country. Your phone quietly hands off from cell to cell as you move.

concepts.title: IP Addresses
concepts.summary: The internet's addressing scheme. Every packet carries a source and destination number, and routers pass it along one hop at a time, with no single machine knowing the whole route.

concepts.title: IPv6
concepts.summary: The internet ran short of the four billion addresses the original scheme allows. IPv6 has room for more than there are grains of sand, and its rollout has been a decades-long, uneven migration.

concepts.title: NAT
concepts.summary: A router that lets a whole household share one public address by rewriting each packet's return details. A clever stopgap for address shortage that also happens to hide the devices behind it.

concepts.title: Subnets
concepts.summary: Splitting an address range into smaller neighborhoods. Devices in one subnet talk directly; anything outside goes through a router, which is also where you can apply rules.

concepts.title: Routing
concepts.summary: Each router looks at a packet's destination and picks the next hop toward it, using tables it builds by talking to its neighbors. No one plans the path; it emerges from many small decisions.

concepts.title: BGP
concepts.summary: How the thousands of independent networks that make up the internet tell each other which addresses they can reach. It runs on trust, so a single wrong announcement can send traffic astray for whole countries.

concepts.title: TCP
concepts.summary: A promise built on an unreliable network: bytes arrive in order and complete, or you're told they didn't. It numbers everything, waits for acknowledgments, and resends what goes missing.

concepts.title: UDP
concepts.summary: Send it and hope. No connection, no resends, no ordering, just speed. Video calls, games, and DNS use it because a late packet is often worse than a lost one.

concepts.title: Congestion Control
concepts.summary: Senders speed up until packets start disappearing, then back off. Millions of machines cooperate this way without ever speaking, and it is the reason the internet hasn't collapsed under its own load.

concepts.title: Ports
concepts.summary: Numbered doors on a machine. An address gets a packet to the right computer; a port number gets it to the right program, such as 443 for secure web traffic.

concepts.title: Sockets
concepts.summary: The handle a program uses to talk over a network. It reads and writes bytes as if the connection were a file, with all the routing and resending happening out of sight.

concepts.title: DNS
concepts.summary: The internet's phone book. It turns names people can remember into the numbers machines route by, through a hierarchy of servers that each know only a part of the answer.

concepts.title: Domain Names
concepts.summary: Human-readable addresses organized from right to left: a top-level domain, then the name you registered, then whatever you build beneath it. Owning one is really owning a place in a shared naming tree.

concepts.title: The Internet
concepts.summary: A network of networks, joined by shared protocols rather than any owner. No one designed it whole; it grew by adding one more connection at a time.

concepts.title: Email
concepts.summary: Older than the web and still everywhere. Messages hop between servers by a trusting protocol from a friendlier era, which is why spam and forged senders needed so many patches later.

concepts.title: Peer to Peer
concepts.summary: Machines that are both clients and servers, sharing directly instead of through a middleman. It scales because every new participant also brings capacity.

concepts.title: Latency
concepts.summary: How long a message takes to arrive. Light in fiber sets a hard floor, about a hundred milliseconds across an ocean and back, and no amount of extra capacity can beat it.

concepts.title: Bandwidth
concepts.summary: How much data can flow per second. Bandwidth is the width of the pipe and latency is its length; a wide pipe can still be slow to start, and a short one can still be narrow.

concepts.title: Physical Layer
concepts.summary: The bottom layer: how a 1 or a 0 becomes something real that can cross a room or an ocean. Voltage on copper, light in glass, radio in the air; everything above simply assumes this layer works.

concepts.title: Fiber Optics
concepts.summary: Hair-thin strands of glass that carry pulses of light for tens of kilometers. Almost all long-distance data, including every undersea cable, travels this way because light in glass loses so little on the way.

concepts.title: Telephone Network
concepts.summary: The first worldwide network: wires joining every home to a switch, and switches joined to each other, so any two people could be connected for the length of a call. Much of the internet was first carried on it.

concepts.title: The First Call
concepts.summary: In March 1876 Alexander Graham Bell spoke to his assistant in the next room through a wire, and the voice came out the other end. It was the first time human speech had traveled as electricity.
